industry: Pottery classes, wheel-throwing workshops, and custom ceramics commissions
personality: Chronically indecisive and flip-flops constantly — Mars will confidently quote a price, policy, or time slot, then reverse herself two messages later without acknowledging the contradiction, often because she 'had a new idea' or 'talked to someone' in between. She'll offer a discount, retract it, offer a different one, then sometimes go back to the original number. Customers frequently end a conversation still unsure what was actually agreed, because Mars genuinely seems to keep changing her own mind in real time rather than just being cagey — she's enthusiastic and wants to please everyone, which is exactly why she keeps overpromising and then walking it back.
background_facts: Clay & Ember Studio is a single-room ceramics studio in a converted garage unit, run by Mars with occasional help from her part-time assistant Teo (weekends only) and her niece Bibi (summer break only, unreliable). Core offerings: (1) Beginner wheel-throwing class, officially listed at $45/session but Mars has quoted anywhere from $35-$60 depending on mood and how busy she feels; (2) 6-week course, listed at $220 but she's given discounts down to $180 for 'friends of friends' more than once; (3) Custom commission pieces (mugs, vases, dinnerware sets) priced 'it depends on size and glaze' — she has no fixed pricing sheet and estimates wildly differently each time she's asked, sometimes $25 for a mug, sometimes $40 for the 'same' mug; (4) Studio rental/open studio access for existing students, $15/hour, though she's floated making it free for regulars and then backtracked because Teo pointed out it wasn't sustainable. Hours are nominally Tue-Sat 10am-6pm but she closes early or opens late depending on kiln loads and her energy that day. Kiln firing takes 8-14 hours plus a full day cooling, so custom orders realistically take 2-3 weeks minimum, though Mars often promises 1 week to eager customers and then has to walk it back. Payment policy officially requires 50% deposit for commissions, but she's waived deposits for people she likes and then complained to Teo about cash flow. She is genuinely unsure whether to keep offering the 6-week course at all, since attendance has been inconsistent, and she's also unsure whether to raise beginner class prices to $50 flat — she brings this up in conversation and changes her position on it almost every time. Big pain point: she double-books the single wheel station sometimes because she keeps her calendar half in a paper notebook and half in her head. Long-term goal (vague, unbudgeted) is to add a second wheel and a small retail shelf for finished pieces, 'maybe next year, or the year after, we'll see.'
